subject: Oceanography
title: Turbidity Currents
description: A quick win: understand Turbidity Currents.

hook.text: In 1929, an earthquake off Newfoundland snapped 12 transatlantic cables one by one—heading downslope.

buildup.text: A turbidity current—a fast-moving avalanche of sediment-laden water—raced down the continental slope.

discovery.text: Scientists timed the cable breaks and calculated the current moved at 70 km/h—faster than a ship.

twist.text: Turbidity currents carve submarine canyons as deep as the Grand Canyon—entirely underwater.

climax.text: They deposit thick sediment fans at the base of slopes—the largest sedimentary features on Earth.

punchline.text: Underwater avalanches carve canyons no one can see.

quiz.question: How was the speed of turbidity currents first measured?
options: By timing sequential transatlantic cable breaks
